opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was one of the more interesting challenges we ran into early on. The way Glaze works is that we compute a perturbation, a set of small changes to the pixels, that shifts how a model's feature extractor perceives the artwork's style, while keeping those changes as unobtrusive as possible to the human eye. And the amount of change we can hide depends a lot on what's already in the image.

If you have a painting with a lot of texture, brushstrokes, canvas grain, color variation, busy backgrounds, there's a lot of visual noise for the perturbation to blend into. The human visual system is pretty forgiving there. You can make fairly significant changes and people just don't notice, because their eye reads it as part of the texture.

Smooth digital art is basically the opposite case. Think flat color fills, clean gradients, anime-style or cel-shaded work, minimalist vector-like illustrations. Large areas of the image are almost perfectly uniform. Any change you introduce into a flat region of solid color stands out immediately. Even a very small amount of perturbation can show up as artifacts, a kind of shimmer or blotchiness, and artists who work in that style are very sensitive to it, understandably, because the cleanness is the whole aesthetic.

So you end up in a tough tradeoff. To get robust protection you need enough perturbation to actually move the style in feature space, but the visual budget you have before it becomes objectionable is much smaller for those images. We did a lot of work on the perceptual side, on how we measure and constrain visible change, and on letting artists choose intensity levels. But it's fair to say that smooth, flat styles have always been the hardest case, where artists have to weigh a bit more visible change against stronger protection.

r001.rationale: It says smooth digital art has flat, uniform regions where even a very small perturbation can create noticeable artifacts; clean gradients are included among the examples.

r002.rationale: It describes keeping perturbations unobtrusive and says textured areas can conceal them, but does not state that Glaze was optimized to place or hide perturbations in less noticeable parts of smooth artwork.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that was actually one of the first things we ran into. Glaze works by adding these small perturbations to the image, little shifts in pixel values that are designed to push the style features in the model's representation space toward some other target style. The thing is, those perturbations have to go somewhere. If you've got an oil painting or something with a lot of texture, heavy brushstrokes, grain, noise, there's a lot of visual "stuff" already there, and the perturbation just kind of blends in. The human eye doesn't notice it because the image is already busy.

But a lot of digital art, especially anime-style work or vector-ish illustration, is the opposite. You have these big flat regions of a single color, really clean gradients, very smooth skin tones. There's nowhere for the perturbation to hide. Any change you make to a flat region, even a tiny one, shows up as this faint speckling or shimmer, and artists are extremely sensitive to that. These are people who spend hours getting a gradient exactly right, so they'll see it immediately.

So we were caught in this tension. If you crank the perturbation budget down low enough that it's invisible on a smooth image, you often don't shift the style features enough to actually confuse the model. And if you keep it high enough to be effective, the artifacts become visible and some artists just won't use it. A lot of the engineering work went into trying to be smarter about where the perturbation goes, putting more of it into edges and areas with existing detail and less into flat regions, and then giving artists a slider so they could choose their own tradeoff between protection strength and visual impact. But I'd be honest and say that smooth styles are still the harder case. It's a fundamental constraint of the approach, not just something we hadn't tuned yet.

r001.rationale: It says tiny changes in flat regions and clean gradients show up as faint speckling or shimmer.

r002.rationale: It says engineering work aimed to put more perturbation into edges and detailed areas and less into flat regions, hiding it where it is less noticeable.

astra-6.text: Smooth digital art gives us less visual texture to hide the perturbations in. With a heavily textured painting, there’s already a lot happening—brushstrokes, variations in color—and small changes can blend into that. But with clean lines and broad regions of smooth color, even a small change can stand out. So the challenge was getting enough of a change to affect how the model learns the style while keeping that change unobtrusive to the person looking at the artwork.

r001.rationale: The response says that on smooth color regions, even a small change can stand out.

r002.rationale: It describes the challenge of keeping changes unobtrusive, but does not state that Glaze’s algorithm was optimized to place or hide perturbations in less noticeable parts of smooth artwork.

sol-6.1.text: Smooth digital art gives us less room to hide the changes that Glaze needs to make. If a painting has a lot of texture or intricate detail, small perturbations can blend into that. But if you have a clean patch of color, a smooth gradient, or very crisp lines, even a small change can stand out. So the challenge is making the image look sufficiently different to the model while keeping it looking the same to a human. For those smoother styles, that balance is much harder to achieve.

r001.rationale: It says even a small change can stand out in a smooth gradient, clearly conveying that tiny Glaze-induced changes are visually noticeable.

r002.rationale: It explains that texture can conceal perturbations and smooth areas make them noticeable, but does not state that Glaze’s algorithm was optimized to place perturbations in less noticeable parts of smooth artwork.
